claim: The agent.png image illustrates that agents are typically implemented as an LLM performing actions using tools, operating in continuous feedback loops, and used in situations where problems and solutions are unpredictable.

The image visually represents that agents have more autonomy than workflows and can make decisions about the tools they use and how to solve problems, while still allowing definition of the available toolset and guidelines for agent behavior.
To use TrackingState with a node-style hook to update agent state after a model call, define a custom AgentState subclass with the desired state fields, such as model_call_count.
Then, create an after_model node-style hook decorated with @after_model and specify the state_schema as TrackingState.
Inside the after_model hook function, accept the current state and runtime as parameters and return a dictionary with the updated state fields, for example incrementing model_call_count by 1.
The returned dictionary from the node-style hook is merged into the agent state using the graph's reducers, updating the agent state accordingly.
The different response_format options that use StructuredResponseT in LangChain are: ToolStrategy[StructuredResponseT], ProviderStrategy[StructuredResponseT], type[StructuredResponseT], and None.
ToolStrategy[StructuredResponseT] uses tool calling for structured output.
ProviderStrategy[StructuredResponseT] uses provider-native structured output.
type[StructuredResponseT] is a schema type that automatically selects the best strategy based on model capabilities.
None means structured output is not explicitly requested.
The store_based_model middleware selects which model to use for a request by reading the user's preferred model from the Store using the user_id from the request's runtime context.
If the user's preferred model is found in the Store and is present in the predefined MODEL_MAP, the middleware overrides the request's model with the preferred model from MODEL_MAP.
If no preferred model is found or it is not in MODEL_MAP, the middleware does not change the model and proceeds with the original request model.
To update model profiles using data from models.dev in LangChain, first update the source data at models.dev through a pull request to its GitHub repository if needed.
Next, update additional fields and overrides in the file langchain_<package>/data/profile_augmentations.toml through a pull request to the LangChain integration package if needed.

Then, use the langchain-model-profiles CLI tool to pull the latest data from models.dev, merge in the augmentations, and update the profile data by running the command: langchain-profiles refresh --provider <provider> --data-dir <data_dir>.

This command downloads the latest data for the specified provider from models.dev, merges augmentations from profile_augmentations.toml in the specified data directory, and writes merged profiles to _profiles.py in that directory.
An example command to refresh profiles for the 'anthropic' provider is: uv run --with langchain-model-profiles langchain-profiles refresh --provider anthropic --data-dir langchain_anthropic/data.
The value function in reasoning_fig7 is used to assess the quality of reasoning steps and to search over multiple reasoning trajectories.
This approach improves reliability by generating a set of answers and then using the value function to pick the best one, rather than generating a single answer from the model.
The summarization_prompt is a text prompt that instructs the model to summarize an article about an invention following a specific schema.
It describes the parameters that the summary should include, such as invented_year, summary, inventors, concepts, and description.
The prompt is used as the system message content in a chat completion request to guide the model's output to match the structured ArticleSummary format.
This structured summarization approach is useful for transforming text content into a structured object for display or database population.
You can build React UIs for real-time agent interactions using LangChain's frontend streaming capabilities with the @useStream hook.
LangChain supports streaming tokens directly from a chat model and streaming agent progress in real-time, which can be integrated into React UIs.
You can trace each step of a conversational loop, debug tool calls, and evaluate agent outputs with LangSmith.
To get set up for tracing, follow the tracing quickstart guide at /langsmith/trace-with-langchain.
It is recommended to also set up LangSmith Engine, which monitors your traces, detects issues, and proposes fixes.
Invoke an agent with a message and pass a thread_id so the agent can persist and resume conversation history, enabling tracing of the conversation state.
To enable LangSmith tracing, set environment variables LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY with your API key.
Chat models accept context as a sequence of message objects, which include system instructions and human inputs, forming a growing list of messages over time.
Because context windows are limited, applications often use techniques to remove or "forget" stale information to manage the growing message list.
Interactions with chat models are often stateless, so each model invocation involves passing the entire accumulated list of messages as input.
Multi-turn agents accumulate long message histories, and tools like LangSmith can record each turn, tool result, and model response for inspection.
Model context includes the full list of messages (conversation history) sent to the model, along with system prompts, tools, model configuration, and response format.

Transient updates can modify messages sent to the model for a single call without changing saved state, while persistent updates modify the conversation history state using lifecycle hooks or commands.
LangChain standardizes model inputs and outputs to handle different provider-specific APIs and message formats, making it easy for developers to switch between models without lock-in.

For structured output, LangChain uses the `response_format` parameter to control how the agent returns structured data, supporting strategies like `ToolStrategy` for tool calling and `ProviderStrategy` for provider-native structured output.

When a schema type is provided directly for structured output, LangChain automatically selects `ProviderStrategy` if the model and provider support native structured output (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI), otherwise it uses `ToolStrategy`.

LangChain normalizes provider-specific streaming formats (such as Anthropic's `thinking` blocks or OpenAI's `reasoning` summaries) into a standard `reasoning` content block type via the `content_blocks` property.
Provider-specific content blocks and escape hatches exist as `NonStandardContentBlock` with type `non_standard` to handle experimental or unique provider features.

You can customize a chat model's input size and capabilities by providing a custom model profile dictionary when initializing the chat model, specifying parameters such as 'max_input_tokens', 'tool_calling', and 'structured_output'.
A custom profile can be passed to the 'init_chat_model' function using the 'profile' parameter to overwrite or update model profile data.
Chat models accept parameters that configure behavior, including model name, provider, authentication key, randomness (temperature), and maximum tokens for output length.
You can create runtime-configurable models by specifying configurable fields such as 'model', 'model_provider', 'temperature', and 'max_tokens', allowing dynamic changes to model parameters.

Defining essential connections in a graph-based system allows nodes to handle their own routing logic, keeping control flow explicit and traceable so the next action is always understandable by looking at the current node.

Edges define how logic is routed and how the graph decides to stop, with types including normal edges for static routing and conditional edges for dynamic routing, affecting how nodes communicate and control flow proceeds.
A node can have multiple outgoing edges, and if so, all destination nodes execute in parallel in the next superstep, influencing control flow concurrency.
Choosing one routing mechanism per node—either normal edges or conditional edges/Command—is important to avoid mixed paths that complicate reasoning about graph behavior and control flow.
Conditional edges use routing functions that determine which node(s) to route to next after execution, enabling optional routing or termination and thus dynamic control flow.
Nodes declare possible next nodes using type hints with Command objects, making routing explicit and traceable, which structures control flow clearly within the graph.
Using Command objects in nodes allows combining state updates and routing decisions in a single function, enabling both control flow and state changes to be managed together.
Conditional entry points allow starting at different nodes based on custom logic, affecting initial control flow routing in the graph.

A system can keep track of conversation history without exceeding the model's input size limit by managing short-term memory with strategies such as trimming messages, deleting messages from state, summarizing messages, managing checkpoints, or using custom strategies like message filtering.

Summarization middleware can be used to automatically condense conversation history when it gets too long by summarizing older messages and replacing them with a summary that is permanently saved for future turns, while keeping recent messages intact.

Summarization middleware triggers based on thresholds such as token count or message count and controls how much context to preserve after summarization by specifying a fraction, token count, or number of recent messages to keep.
Trimming messages involves removing the first or last N messages before calling the LLM to keep the message history within the context window without deleting messages from state.

GPT enhances finding relevant information from large amounts of data by combining generative capabilities with retrieval components that access large corpora, enabling suggestions based on wide-ranging knowledge.
GPT can answer questions about unfamiliar topics by using a two-step Search-Ask method: first searching a library of text for relevant sections, then asking GPT with the retrieved text.
GPT can augment existing search systems by mimicking human browsing behavior and by retrieval with embeddings, which finds content most related to a query using cosine similarity.
Because GPT models have a limited maximum text length they can process at once, using a Search-Ask approach is recommended to draw upon large quantities of text.
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) allows fetching relevant information from a database to generate answers, reducing hallucinations and providing up-to-date, relevant information.
The email agent uses a node called 'Classify Intent' which employs a large language model (LLM) to analyze the email content and classify its intent, urgency, topic, and summary.
The classification is done by invoking a structured LLM with a prompt containing the email content and sender email, which returns a structured dictionary with the classification results.

Based on the classification's 'intent' and 'urgency' fields, the agent decides the next action node to route to: if intent is 'billing' or urgency is 'critical', it routes to 'human_review'; if intent is 'question' or 'feature', it routes to 'search_documentation'; if intent is 'bug', it routes to 'bug_tracking'; otherwise, it routes to 'draft_response'.

You can handle exceptions during tool execution by using LangChain agent middleware that wraps the tool call and converts exceptions into ToolMessages the model can handle, preventing the agent from stopping.

An example middleware function named handle_tool_errors catches exceptions during tool calls and returns a ToolMessage with an error content prompting to check input and try again, including the exception message.
This middleware is applied when creating the agent by passing it in the middleware parameter of create_agent, allowing the agent to continue running and retry with corrected inputs.

Alternatively, you can customize error handling using the handle_errors parameter in ToolStrategy to provide a custom error message or specify exception types on which to retry, enabling retries with corrected inputs.
A super-step in LangGraph is a single 'tick' of the graph where all nodes scheduled for that step execute, potentially in parallel.
In a sequential graph, each node or step corresponds to a separate super-step, producing a checkpoint after each one.
LangGraph creates a checkpoint at each super-step boundary, which is a full state snapshot that can be used to resume execution.
Within a super-step, writes from individual node executions are persisted as tasks, enabling recovery of successful nodes' outputs if another node in the same super-step fails.
Execution can only be resumed from a checkpoint at a super-step boundary, not mid-function inside a node.
When resuming execution after an interrupt or retry, the affected node runs again from the start of its function, so node logic should be idempotent.
You can handle user input during a continuous event processing loop in LangGraph by using event streaming with human-in-the-loop (HITL) interrupts.

Use the typed projections returned by graph.stream_events(..., version="v3") in a loop until the run finishes, streaming AI responses token-by-token via stream.messages, observing per-step state snapshots via stream.values, detecting interrupts via stream.interrupted and reading their payloads from stream.interrupts.

When an interrupt is detected (stream.interrupted is true), read the interrupt payload from stream.interrupts, get user input based on the interrupt info, then resume execution by calling stream_events again with Command(resume=user_response) and repeat until stream.interrupted is false.

A typical code pattern involves initializing stream_input with the initial input, then in a while loop calling graph.stream_events(stream_input, config=config, version="v3"), streaming message chunks as they arrive, checking for interrupts after the run finishes or pauses, and if interrupted, getting user input and setting stream_input to Command(resume=user_response) to resume.
You can configure a node to retry an operation multiple times by passing a RetryPolicy to the retry_policy parameter of add_node.

RetryPolicy has parameters such as max_attempts to set the maximum number of attempts including the first, initial_interval for seconds before the first retry, backoff_factor to multiply the interval after each retry, max_interval for maximum seconds between retries, jitter to add random jitter, and retry_on to specify exceptions to retry on.
The retry policy automatically re-runs a failed node attempt based on exception type and backoff settings.
Retries are part of fault tolerance mechanisms that LangGraph provides to respond to node failures, including retries, timeouts, and error handling.
You can handle process termination signals like SIGTERM by using a RunControl object from langgraph.runtime and calling its request_drain() method to signal the program to stop gracefully.
A recommended pattern is to set a signal handler for SIGTERM that calls control.request_drain("sigterm"), allowing the program to finish ongoing tasks before exiting.

When request_drain() is called, it does not cancel running asyncio tasks or kill threads, so for a hard upper bound on shutdown time, you should pair drain with a graceful timeout and task cancellation.
If the program is stopped early due to drain, it raises a GraphDrained exception, which you can catch to handle the shutdown and optionally resume later with the same configuration.
The core agent loop involves calling a model, letting it choose tools to execute, and finishing when it calls no more tools.

A typical agent loop consists of two main steps: 1) Model call - calls the LLM with a prompt and available tools, returns either a response or a request to execute tools; 2) Tool execution - executes the tools that the LLM requested, returns tool results.
This loop continues until the LLM decides to finish.
Middleware exposes hooks before and after each of the core agent loop steps.
Middleware provides two styles of hooks to intercept agent execution: node-style hooks and wrap-style hooks.
Node-style hooks run sequentially at specific execution points such as before the agent starts, before each model call, after each model response, and after the agent completes.
Wrap-style hooks run around each call, giving control over execution, such as around each model call and around each tool call.

Middleware allows hooking into any step in the agent lifecycle to update context (modify state, update conversation history, save insights) or jump in the lifecycle (skip steps or repeat calls based on context).
